strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile computer-vision problem: editing emotion-associated image content while preserving the scene. Conditioning on only a source image and target emotion offers a useful interface, and several examples demonstrate changes beyond color or texture transfer.

EmoPair is a potentially useful resource comprising 338,544 image pairs, including 6,949 specifically generated emotion-editing pairs. The manuscript credits InstructPix2Pix and EmoSet and documents the construction pipeline and filtering criteria.

The evaluation includes randomized human comparisons, emotion-transition breakdowns, and component and iteration ablations. The reported 56% overall online preference provides some evidence of perceptual benefit beyond agreement with an emotion classifier.

The figures communicate the pipeline effectively. The explicit discussion of semantic drift, facial artifacts, and potential misuse is constructive; the human study also reports informed consent and institutional approval.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evidence is strongly coupled to the inference procedure. The same predictor P labels training data, selects outputs over up to 30 editing iterations, and supplies EMR and ESR. Table 1 shows EMR falling from 50.20% to 5.06% without P, so the improvement cannot be cleanly attributed to the learned editor rather than predictor-directed search. Independent evaluation, human assessment of ablations, and baselines using the same selection procedure and generation budget are needed.

The comparisons support narrower conclusions than the claimed general superiority. InstructPix2Pix receives single-word prompts already acknowledged to be ineffective, and the closely related Affective Image Filter is cited but not evaluated. Against the stronger LMS baseline, human preference is 54% online, 50% for transitions to positive emotions, and 49% in the small laboratory study (Fig. S7). These results show promise but do not establish a substantial, consistent advantage.

The training formulation leaves a consequential ambiguity. Section 3.2 defines z = E(Is), corrupts this source latent, and uses the source again as conditioning in the denoising loss; the paired target image never appears explicitly. Taken literally, this trains source reconstruction. The manuscript needs corrected equations or pseudocode explaining target supervision. Supplement S2.2 also omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, dataset mixing, and key sampling settings, limiting reproducibility despite the promised release.

The proposed metrics require stronger justification. As written, KL(eg || eoh) in ESR is infinite whenever a predicted distribution assigns positive probability outside the one-hot target; the implemented direction or smoothing must be specified. Furthermore, Grad-CAM-based pixel differences and Canny-edge differences do not establish semantic preservation. The human experiment evaluates emotion preference without jointly assessing preservation, leaving a central task requirement insufficiently validated.

The architectural and reasoning claims exceed what is demonstrated. The global/local design is insufficiently distinguished from existing image-conditioned diffusion editing. Because the emotion encoder receives only an eight-category label, it produces eight source-independent embeddings; cosine alignment with instruction embeddings does not itself demonstrate image-specific instruction inference or human-like neuro-symbolic reasoning. A simpler learned-label-conditioning baseline would help establish the contribution of this design.

Dataset quality and generalization remain insufficiently characterized. Approximately 98% of EmoPair consists of existing pairs automatically labeled by P, whose reported 73% accuracy on EmoSet does not validate labels on these synthetic pairs. Human ranking of generic prompts does not establish per-pair annotation quality. A human audit, emotion-transition statistics, and separate subset ablations would strengthen the dataset contribution. Same-valence and neutral-image generalization are supported only by selected examples.

The human-study reporting needs clarification. The stated 417 participants × 100 trials equals 41,700, rather than 417,000; this arithmetic error is readily correctable. More substantively, only about 27% of online participants pass screening, making explicit final sample counts, sensitivity to filtering, and an explanation of how standard errors account for repeated participants and images important for interpreting the modest preference margins.
